speaker: Siddhartha Mukherjee
title: The Alarming New Risks of Cancer Everyone Needs to Hear
question: With breast cancer rising in younger women, why don't oncologists simply start universal routine mammograms in a woman's thirties?
guest: The problem with mammograms is that the yield to discover a real cancer is very low, especially in young women, and that's complicated by women who have dense breasts. By yield, I mean how many mammograms you need to take in order to save one breast cancer life. Even leaving aside dense breasts, which is particularly common in young women, the yield in a mammogram is very low in that group. Doing mammograms early or doing more mammograms will inevitably yield lots of false positives, lots more biopsies, and lots more anxiety, alongside only a few real cases. So what I recommend is that if you're a young woman with a family history of breast, ovarian, or pancreatic cancer, see a physician for genetic counseling to check for BRCA1, BRCA2, and other mutations. Even if you aren't BRCA-positive, there's a polygenic risk score that estimates your genetic risk, and women at high risk can enroll in intensive screening using alternating MRI and mammograms or MRI alone.

Because for average-risk women in their thirties, the harms of screening would outweigh the benefits, even with incidence rising.

Although rates are climbing, the absolute risk remains low: roughly 1 in 200 women will be diagnosed during their thirties, versus about 1 in 40 in their sixties. Screening millions to find few cancers means the vast majority of abnormal results are false alarms, leading to anxiety, repeat imaging, and unnecessary biopsies.

Mammography also works worse in younger women. Their breast tissue is denser, which hides tumours and lowers sensitivity. Cancers in this age group are also more often fast-growing, so they tend to appear between screens. There is also overdiagnosis, a small cumulative radiation risk from starting earlier, and no trial evidence that screening in the thirties reduces deaths.

So the approach is risk-based instead. Guidelines such as the US Preventive Services Task Force now start average-risk screening at 40, and experts urge formal risk assessment by about age 25 to 30. Women at high risk (BRCA carriers, strong family history, prior chest radiation) do start earlier, often with MRI added to mammography.

models.answer: Although breast cancer rates are rising in women under 40, universal mammography in a woman’s thirties would cause more harm than benefit because absolute incidence in this age group remains low. When a disease is relatively uncommon, broad screening has a low positive predictive value, meaning the vast majority of suspicious findings are false alarms. Compounding this, younger women typically have dense breast tissue that appears white on mammograms just like tumors, simultaneously masking real cancers and inflating false positives. Screening millions of average-risk women in their thirties would trigger vast numbers of callbacks, anxiety, unnecessary biopsies, and overdiagnosis, while adding a decade of cumulative radiation exposure to younger, more radiosensitive breast tissue. Moreover, no clinical trials have shown that routine mammograms before age 40 reduce mortality, partly because tumors in young women often grow rapidly and emerge between scheduled scans. Instead of universal screening, medical guidelines recommend formal risk assessment by age 25 to 30 so high-risk women can begin targeted early MRIs and mammograms.

noweb.answer: Universal mammography in a woman’s thirties is not recommended because, for average-risk women that age, the harms outweigh the benefits. Younger women typically have dense breast tissue, which appears white on a mammogram just like tumors, lowering accuracy by masking real cancers while triggering frequent false alarms. Moreover, although incidence is rising, the absolute risk of breast cancer in one’s thirties remains relatively low. Screening a low-prevalence population produces far more false positives than true detections, subjecting thousands of healthy women to anxiety, costly follow-up scans, invasive biopsies, and overdiagnosis of slow-growing lesions that would never threaten their lives, all without proven evidence of reducing overall mortality. Starting routine X-rays a decade earlier also increases cumulative lifetime radiation exposure to younger breast tissue, which is more vulnerable to radiation-induced DNA damage. Rather than screening everyone, oncology guidelines recommend a formal risk assessment between ages twenty-five and thirty so women with genetic mutations, strong family histories, or other risk factors receive targeted early screening—often including breast MRI—while sparing average-risk women unnecessary harm.

The main reason is that the absolute risk in women in their thirties is still low, even though incidence is rising. Rates among women under 50 have gone up by roughly 1–2% a year. Even so, only about 1 in 200 women develops breast cancer between ages 30 and 40.

Screening everyone in that group would mean many tests for each cancer found, and mammography works less well in younger women. Their breasts tend to be dense, which hides tumors and lowers sensitivity. Density also produces more false positives, so many healthy women would get callbacks, biopsies and anxiety. There would also be some overdiagnosis of lesions that would never have caused harm, plus small amounts of radiation added up over years. No randomized trial has shown that screening in the thirties reduces deaths, so the trade-off isn't clearly favorable.

Guidelines respond with risk-based screening instead. In 2024 the USPSTF lowered the starting age to 40, every two years. The American College of Radiology recommends a risk assessment by age 25 so that high-risk women can start earlier, usually with MRI around age 25–30. That group includes carriers of BRCA or other gene variants, women who had chest radiation, and women with strong family histories. Women of any age with symptoms such as a lump should get a diagnostic workup rather than wait for screening.
